Subject: Next steps: Dedicated trial & hyperscaler comparison

Hi Julie / Peter —

Thanks again for taking the demo today. Quick recap and a concrete proposal so we can move to a short comparative trial. Key takeaways from our call: you want predictable latency at tail (99/99.9), cost visibility, and clear capacity guarantees for peak traffic. You also want a direct apples-to-apples comparison vs the hyperscaler endpoints you currently run.

Proposed next steps (suggested 2-week lab trial):
- Test matrix: throughput (QPS), 95/99/99.9 latency under target load, failover/region-cutover, and cost-per-1k-tokens for typical prompt mixes.
- Workload: run your real inference traces (we can use the sample you shared) plus a synthetic burst pattern to emulate launch-day peaks.
- Dedicated config: provision a reserved dedicated GPU pool that matches the vCPU/GPU class you asked about; we'll hold capacity for the trial window and provide a per-token pricing sheet.
- Hyperscaler comparison: we will run equivalent tests on the hyperscaler config you listed (reserved instances / committed use) so the comparison includes provisioning latency, scaling behavior, and actual tail latency under identical workloads.

Attachments: redwood-dedicated-vs-hyperscaler-one-pager.pdf, datacorps-workload-sample.json (please confirm this sample is OK for the tests).

Can you confirm:
1) the target peak QPS you want to validate (your note said ~120 QPS sustained with spikes to 450),
2) whether multi-region failover matters for the scope, and
3) any compliance constraints for running the synthetic traces?

If that looks good I’ll loop in Engineering (Monica) to draft a short test plan and Rishi to provide a trial agreement. Recommended kickoff: May 31, 10:00 AM PT for a 30-minute alignment call.

—Sean

Julie —

Thanks for confirming. Quick technical notes and what we’ll include in the trial pack:

What "dedicated" means for the trial:
- We provision a reserved GPU pool for your account for the trial window. Capacity is pinned to the pool (no eviction) so you get predictable throughput/latency.
- Autoscaling can be configured but will be constrained to the reserved-capacity envelope you approve; this avoids surprises baseline vs peak.

Key differences vs hyperscaler reserved VMs:
- Kernel & runtime: our serving runtime uses continuous batching + KV cache pinning; this usually yields lower per-token latency for the same GPU spec compared to a generic VM-managed endpoint.
- Cold-starts & KV warm-up: we pre-warm popular prefixes and can persist KV cache across warm restarts for the trial (helps tail latency during failovers).
- Fallbacks: if the reserved pool is saturated, we can route overflow to a compatible quantized model variant — this keeps availability high while bounding cost.

Proposed test matrix (we’ll run these in order):
1) Canary (single-region): 15–30 minute steady-state at 120 QPS, then 5-minute spike to 450 QPS. Collect 50/95/99/99.9 latency and token cost.
2) Multi-region failover: simulate region outage and measure end-to-end session continuity and KV warm-up time.
3) Long-run cost: run a 24-hour baseline simulation to measure real token economics.

I’m attaching a short proposed SLA/trial doc (proposed-trial-sla.pdf) that spells out reserved capacity, measurement windows, and what metrics we’ll capture. Please review and I’ll iterate.

Monica Patel
